title: What Happens Between Individual Productivity and Organizational Gains?
author: Jason L. Zimmerman
summary: Jason Zimmerman, a behavioral economist and founder of 3Fold Collective, examines why AI makes individual employees faster while organizations capture little of the benefit. He cites McKinsey's August survey in which roughly 80 percent reported better personal productivity, only 37 percent saw a positive effect on earnings and just 6 percent qualified as AI high performers. His diagnosis is that individual gains disappear in the workflow, illustrated by an AI-written software development process that looked complete but ignored the company's real routines, which is the kind of output researchers call workslop. He argues that organizations should move from AI adoption to augmentation by decomposing work, making intrinsic knowledge visible and redesigning workflows, noting that nearly three quarters of high performers do this. He offers PMO status reporting and a financial-services call center as examples where AI absorbs coordination work and frees people for judgment. He concludes that AI transformation eventually becomes a workforce question about skills, roles and decision rights.
points: The gap between 80 percent reporting individual gains and 6 percent reaching high-performer status shows that task-level speedups do not automatically become organizational value.
Polished AI output that lacks the organization's intrinsic knowledge shifts the burden of context to whoever receives it, which researchers call workslop.
AI high performers redesign workflows around the technology rather than speeding up isolated tasks like emails and summaries.

The best early targets are workflows heavy in coordination, repeated information searches and manual reconciliation, because removing them frees meaningful blocks of time rather than scattered minutes.
Redesigned work changes jobs, so leaders must invest in skills, roles and decision rights alongside the tools.
quotes: Only 37% reported any positive impact on their organization’s earnings. And just 6% qualify as what McKinsey calls “AI high performers,” organizations gaining at least 5% on EBIT from AI.
Somewhere between the employee writing Mark a better email and the company realizing financial benefits, a sizeable chunk of organizational-level productivity disappears.
AI-generated work that looks polished and complete, but leaves the real thinking and cleanup to whoever receives it.

So while AI had produced a credible SDLC. It just hadn’t produced their SDLC. And because the document looked finished, the burden of supplying all that missing context moved to the people downstream.
When AI cannot see the context embedded in that system, it can make one task faster while making the larger system work harder.
Once the work is pulled apart, the organization has to make visible what has historically remained intrinsic.
An employee cannot redeploy five minutes here and twelve minutes there into anything that produces organizational-level gains.
The companies that capture its value will probably not be the ones whose employees generate the most tokens, write the most prompts, or save the most isolated minutes.
